title: Indrik Spider
summary: Indrik Spider is a financially motivated cybercrime group tracked under several names, including Evil Corp, Manatee Tempest, DEV-0243 and UNC2165. Public reporting links it to large-scale banking trojan campaigns from around 2014 and to later ransomware activity. The group is documented as using the Dridex banking trojan to steal credentials and move through networks, and it has run ransomware families such as BitPaymer, WastedLocker, Hades and Phoenix Locker. The United States government sanctioned the group and named individuals in 2019, and further actions against suspected members were reported in 2024. Analysts note that the group adapted its tools and branding in response. Evidence in a victim environment includes credential theft from mail clients, remote management tools installed on endpoints, deleted shadow copies and mass file renaming.

beginner.definition: Indrik Spider is a criminal group that attacks companies for money. It is also known as Evil Corp, Manatee Tempest and other names. Security researchers say it started by stealing bank details with a virus called Dridex. Later, it moved to ransomware, which is software that locks files until a payment is made.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group has attacked many large organisations for more than ten years. It shows how criminals change tools when defenders block them. If a company ignores basic hygiene, such as patching and watching for stolen passwords, this group can enter and spread. Governments have placed sanctions on the group. That means paying them may also break the law, which can harm your company.
howItWorks: The group sends emails with infected documents or links. Opening them installs a banking trojan called Dridex on the computer.
That trojan steals logins and sends them to the attackers. It also lets them load more tools on the machine.
The attackers use the stolen logins to move around the network and find servers that hold valuable data.
They turn off backups and security tools so that recovery becomes hard for the victim.
Finally, they run ransomware, which locks files and shows a message demanding payment.
beginner.example: Imagine a night desk at a hotel. A guest hands over a fake membership card in the lobby. The clerk scans it, and hidden software copies the clerk's master key. Nobody notices for weeks. One night the same visitor returns with the copied key, locks every room from the inside, and leaves a note asking for money. Indrik Spider works that way. Its first tool steals the key quietly, and its later tool locks everything at once.
takeaways: One group can run several malware families and change names over the years.
Sanctions can make paying a ransom a legal problem, not only a business choice.
Protecting backups and watching for stolen logins limits damage from this crime group.

objectives: Explain what Indrik Spider is and why it is described as financially motivated.
Describe the role of the Dridex banking trojan in later ransomware attacks.
List the group's known aliases and recognise the same activity in public reporting.
Explain how stolen credentials and remote management tools support lateral movement.
Summarise how sanctions affect decisions about paying a ransom.
Identify log and endpoint evidence that indicates this group's presence.
